The government scare campaign against Labor 's tax-and-spend agenda was designed to shore up the old class loyalty of voters who own property and shares . The bargain Morrison struck with them was to forgive the Coalition 's stalling on climate change because he would save their franking credits . <p> Intriguingly , one of the subplots in the 2022 campaign has been the appearance of past prime ministers John Howard and Kevin Rudd in the electorates that Morrison dare not set foot in . Perhaps the parties are trying to recreate the vibe of our last normal election , in 2007 , when the contest was between leaders with high approval ratings and the main parties each had primary votes safely above 40 per cent . <p> The Liberals have followed up Howard 's campaign stops with a personalised letter which mentions the elephant in the mansion . <p> " Of course @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the job , " the former prime minister wrote in his missive to voters in Higgins . " However , in these uncertain times , he and his Liberal team are the best choice to ensure a strong future for our wonderful country . " <p> Howard would recall that in 2007 the then member for Higgins , his treasurer Peter Costello , had removed any reference to the PM from his election material . <h> Divided by place <p> The second irony follows from the first , and it is in the majority that Anthony Albanese is chasing for Labor . Party polling has identified more than twice as many winnable seats in the capitals ( 14 ) as in the regions ( six ) . When you consider the starting point for the campaign was 46 Labor seats in the capitals and just 23 in the regions , the opposition is relying on an electoral map that reinforces the fault line of place . <p> The Coalition holds 30 seats in the capitals , and 46 in the regions . The crossbench has the remaining six seats , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ his goal is to offset any losses in the capitals to Labor or the teals with gains from Labor on the urban fringes and in the regions . <p> Campaigning outside Brisbane City Hall . The divide between capitals and regions , and between the inner cities and outer urban areas , has only sharpened.Credit:Tony Moore <p> How does a country divided along these lines actually function ? <p> There is an unfortunate reflex in our politics -- from those who practice it to those who analyse it for a living -- to seek American or British analogies for our polarisation . But the better framework has always been to view Australia through the oldest lens of settlement , our colonial-era rivalries . <p> Australia 's decades of complacent prosperity in the 1950s and ' 60s , and our reform decade of the 1980s , were exceptions to the rule of division between states . <p> Loading <p> Federal governments were anchored with majorities across Victoria , NSW and Queensland . In the 17 elections held between 1949 and 1987 , the party that formed government won a majority of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and 13 in Queensland . Elections were decided , in effect , in the middle-class suburbs of Melbourne and Sydney . <p> The early ' 90s recession broke that run . In the 11 elections held since 1990 , Queensland has sided with the winner on 10 occasions , NSW eight and Victoria just three times . The simple explanation is that Victoria turned leftward , while power shifted to the north . <p> But the story is more complex . Melbourne and Sydney had , in fact , been moving even closer politically - but apart from the rest of the nation . <p> An early indication of the new cosmopolitan bond was the 1999 republic referendum , where Victoria and NSW recorded above-average Yes votes , while Queensland returned the largest No vote . <p> Howard never won a majority of seats in Melbourne during his four election triumphs between 1996 and 2004 , and always performed relatively worse in his hometown than he did in the rest of NSW and across Queensland . <p> That pattern has repeated over the course of the past three Coalition governments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ majority in Victoria , while Malcolm Turnbull lost both Victoria and NSW in 2016 , as did Morrison in his 2019 " miracle " win . <p> The key across all three terms that allowed the Coalition to retain power over a polarised country was their super-majorities in Queensland and Western Australia . The country was run by prime ministers from Sydney , but on behalf of the frontier states . <p> Turnbull and Morrison were each in their way hostage to the rifts within the Coalition party room . The Queenslanders always threatened to cross the floor against Turnbull , and ultimately led the rebellion which saw Morrison emerge as the compromise candidate over Turnbull 's challenger Peter Dutton . <p> Yet Morrison has been no more effective than Turnbull in managing the tensions between moderates and conservatives within the government . Part of this is due to the reform fight he chose to pick on religious discrimination . He simply never had the numbers . <p> From Sydney , for the frontier : Prime Minister Scott Morrison with Nationals MP Michelle Landry at the Rockhampton Museum of Art @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the five moderates who crossed the floor to defeat that legislation in February -- Katie Allen , Bridget Archer , Fiona Martin , Dave Sharma and Trent Zimmerman . Allen is the member for Higgins , Sharma represents Wentworth and Zimmerman North Sydney -- three of the inner-city seats at risk from teal independents or Labor . Martin is the member for Reid in Sydney 's inner west , while Archer represents Bass , the ultra-marginal seat based around Launceston in Tasmania . Both are also on Labor 's target list . <p> To his credit , Morrison did secure Coalition agreement for a net zero emissions policy by 2050 . But his effort to end climate change wars within the government has been undermined by the same conservative voices from Queensland that vetoed Turnbull on this issue . <p> Here 's the final irony , and it is in Morrison 's own persona as the curry-cooking , rugby league-following man of faith from the suburbs . <p> Loading <h> Splitting the difference <p> Nothing Morrison has done in politics has been subtle . He has the campaign director 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ electoral map . The insight he had in 2019 , when all the polls suggested he would lose , was that the Coalition could protect its majority by picking up seats from Labor in the regions when the tide was already going out on the Liberals in the capitals . <p> He drew that conclusion , in part , from the result of the Marriage Equality postal survey in 2017 , which found Queensland and NSW to be slightly less progressive than the nation at large . Only 17 of the nation 's 151 electorates voted " no " . <p> Morrison took most notice of the 12 that rejected same-sex marriage in NSW . Among them were Bennelong , Parramatta and Gough Whitlam 's old seat of Werriwa , in Sydney 's outer south-west , where Morrison made an unexpected appearance on Thursday . <p> With Perth and even Brisbane threatening to swing to the left , thus joining the other capitals in the Labor column , the only realistic hope for the government 's re-election is a realignment that brings migrants and blue-collar workers from the urban fringes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The problem with this pitch is that it seeks to make a virtue out of what may be the defining issue of the campaign : Morrison 's character . You may not like me , he seems to be saying , but I am more real than the other guy . <p> Loading <p> He makes no effort to bridge any of the divides in the electorate ; on the contrary , he has revelled in them . Morrison presents himself as the everyman standing against cosmopolitan Australia . <p> The question is can a Liberal run against his own base in the city and survive , when the majority in those seats represents the biggest wave in Australian politics today : working women .

@@90921024 <p> The International Chamber of Commerce says governments must " double down " on the global trade agenda and avoid impulses towards onshoring , as supply chains disruptions continue to roil economies . <p> Global supply chains already struggling under the weight of a pandemic-driven spike in demand and heavy rainfall on the east coast and central Australia have been pushed even further since Russia 's invasion of the Ukraine . <p> Former Australian diplomat and ICC head of global engagement Damien Bruckard said the supply chain situation had been " quite extraordinary " over the last two years , with spot rates for shipping containers rising sixfold , turnaround times for ships at ports doubling and a shortage of critical inputs like semiconductors . <p> Since the start of the war in late February , he said lead times had lengthened by about 15 per cent , input prices were up 25 per cent , and energy and food supply chains in particular were facing huge instability . They 're not going to be able to absorb those cost increases in fertiliser prices -- they 're basically going to go out of business and stop producing food , " said Mr Bruckard , who beamed into a Committee for Economic Development of Australia supply chains event on Friday . <p> " Looking at the potential for political and social instability . . . that will bounce back to the advanced economies . @@90921116 <h> Editorial <h> For integrity 's sake , Australia needs a change of government <p> The unusual intervention by 31 retired judges this week calling for a strong national integrity commission was one of the most significant events of the election campaign . The government may believe this is a niche issue of scant interest in the suburbs , and perhaps it is right . But integrity is , in The Age 's view , the overarching theme of this campaign . <p> It is not about an integrity commission in isolation . It is about trust in our political system to act in the public interest , about an insistence that public money be used for public , not political , purposes . It is about accountability for alleged wrongdoing . It is about political donation reform to reduce the risk of wealthy interests buying influence . Whether the issue be taxation reform , climate change , infrastructure or community grants , the integrity of our systems is bedrock . <p> This government has no interest in a strong integrity commission despite its promise at the 2019 election . Its inadequate bill would not allow the agency to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ public . Senior legal figures have said it is not designed to expose corruption , but to cover it up . <p> Whether it be the so-called " sports rorts " grants under which a minister ignored independent advice to funnel millions to Coalition-targeted seats , the commuter car parks promised overwhelmingly to Coalition electorates , or the refusal to hold an inquiry into former attorney-general Christian Porter 's use of anonymous donations to fund his legal fees , the government 's " nothing to see here " responses have normalised wrongdoing as just the way politics works . <p> Overall , this election campaign has been dispiriting because both major parties have conducted intense disagreements over a small range of issues , with neither telling the truth about the big challenges the country faces . <p> But Labor leader Anthony Albanese understands that trust in government has eroded and that it matters . " We need to make sure that we restore faith in the integrity of our political system , " he says about the opposition 's proposal for a strong commission . We would prefer to see @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ things up would begin to dispel the cynical idea that somehow integrity in politics is an oxymoron . <p> The government 's central pitch for a fourth term is that it is the better manager of the economy . The unemployment rate of 3.9 per cent -- the lowest in half a century -- is not entirely the government 's doing , but it deserves some credit . The past three years have been dominated by the pandemic . While the federal government made mistakes , it -- along with the states -- also deserves credit for the decisions made in a fast-moving crisis that meant that we have a low death rate comparatively and , after a tardy start , a high double-dose vaccination rate among adults . <p> Prime Minister Scott Morrison has said that " JobKeeper saved the country " . That one decision to spend tens of billions to subsidise workers ' wages during the worst of the pandemic was the government 's finest achievement , saving hundreds of thousands of jobs , although the scheme was marred by too many companies that did not need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spending was justified to avert an economic and human catastrophe , this election is being fought in the context of endless government deficits . It is a pretence that both sides of politics prosecute -- that we can spend more money on aged care , the NDIS , defence , childcare and training with scant savings and deficits out to the next decade . At some point , the government will need to raise taxes to pay for services the public rightly demands , such as a dignified aged care system , or trim spending elsewhere . <p> Loading <p> We have had a semi-debate about wages and inflation but no serious discussion about tax reform or productivity , although Albanese argues his increased childcare subsidies are aimed at boosting productivity , the key to wages growth . Whichever party forms government , falling real wages , higher interest rates and rising inflation will be the reality . Perhaps then we can talk seriously about productivity that includes cheaper childcare , reforming the tax system and improving education standards . <p> The housing debate has had an air of fantasy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will do anything about housing affordability , because neither wants prices to drop for fear of upsetting existing home owners . The policies tinker around the edges , if anything likely to increase housing prices while doing nothing about the lack of housing supply . <p> Throughout the campaign , the government has failed to make a compelling case for a fourth term . Labor 's agenda may be modest , but it is hard to discern a serious government agenda after nine years of Coalition government . It has shown scant interest in economic and tax reform and is headed by a prime minister who too often has failed to take responsibility until forced to do so . <p> On one issue in particular , Australia can not afford three more years of this government . Neither side of politics is telling the truth about the future of coal , but at least the government 's tired attempts to run another scare campaign on electricity prices fell flat -- it is hard to argue with the Australian Industry Group , the Business Council and the National Farmers ' Federation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Australians have had almost 10 years of a government that has misled the country on climate change , one that has only recently committed to the bare minimum , with some members of the Coalition already undermining that . It supports net zero emissions by 2050 , but has refused to increase its commitment to reduce emissions by 26 to 28 per cent by 2030 . All the evidence is that it is this decade that matters most , and we have little confidence that the Coalition would do more than drag its heels . <p> Labor 's interim target of emission cuts by 43 per cent by 2030 is better , but not ambitious enough , but at least Labor has some plan to get there , including a $20 billion fund to build electricity transmission links . Only the Greens ' target of a 74 per cent reduction by 2030 is judged consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees . <p> An honest campaign would have all sides acknowledging that coal is quickly on its way out and reassuring communities that transition plans are serious . @@90921141 <h> For Australia 's Indian-born voters , Albanese is in favour . For now . <h> By Caroline Duckworth , Devesh Kapur and Milan Vaishnav <p> As Australia heads to the polls , the country 's sizeable immigrant population is likely to substantially influence the outcome . Immigrants account for around 30 per cent of Australia 's population -- the highest fraction among large , Western countries . And no immigrant group has experienced growth as rapid as the Indian diaspora . <p> Between 2010 and 2020 , the number of Indian-born residents more than doubled from approximately 330,000 to 721,000 . Indians now account for nearly 3 per cent of the total population and comprise the second-largest immigrant community in Australia . This influx of Indian migrants also has a significant cultural impact : Hinduism is the country 's fastest growing religion and Punjabi the fastest growing language . <p> Australia 's growing Indian community turns out en masse for the 2018 Boxing Day Test.Credit:Julian Smith <p> It is no wonder then that the diaspora has been courted by nearly all political parties this election . Prime Minister Scott Morrison has garnered attention for his selfies cooking India-flavoured @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pact . Labor Party leader Anthony Albanese too has redoubled his party 's efforts to woo the community , visiting temples and showering praise on their contributions to Australian life . <p> Yet , despite all this newfound attention , we know very little about which way the diaspora will swing on election day . A new , nationally representative survey that we carried out with the research firm , YouGov , offers the first hard data with which to answer this question . The survey , conducted April 4 to April 22 , draws on a sample of 617 Indo-Australians who are registered to vote in the upcoming general election . It has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.9 per cent . <p> The results indicate that four out of 10 Indo-Australians plan to vote for Labor in the general election while about 25 per cent intend to vote for the Coalition . The Greens place third with 15 per cent of the community 's vote . Importantly , one in 10 registered voters was still undecided at the time the survey was conducted . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ curry on Facebook on New Year 's Eve.Credit:Facebook <p> This headline finding cuts against the grain of the received wisdom , which assumes a conservative-minded diaspora that identifies with the right-of-centre Coalition . This assumption is bolstered by the present government 's determined attempts to forge a strategic partnership with the Indian government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi . <p> However , when Indo-Australians are asked to place themselves on a standard left-right ideological spectrum , 58 per cent self-identify with the liberal end of the political spectrum . Data for the Indian diaspora in Canada , the United Kingdom , and the United States reveals that Australia is only second to Canada for the highest proportion of liberal voters . <p> Advertisement <p> The policy issues driving the Indo-Australian vote shed light on this leftward tilt . When asked to rank the most important issues shaping their vote choice , three emerge ( chosen by 13 per cent of respondents each ) : healthcare , the environment and climate change , and the economy . Climate change 's inclusion here is noteworthy . Nearly a quarter of respondents who @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ arguing the Coalition is not sufficiently committed to mitigating climate change . <p> The survey finds little evidence to back up assertions that foreign policy considerations will dominate the voting behaviour of Indo-Australians . To be sure , three-quarters of respondents reported that a party 's position on India is important when deciding who they will support in the general election . But when set against other weighty , kitchen-table issues , only six per cent of respondents reported Australia-India relations was their most pressing election concern . <p> Anthony Albanese visits an Indian temple in Sydney 's Blacktown as part of the Diwali festival in 2021 . Credit:Nick Moir <p> While these topline findings will bring much cheer to Labor supporters , the data suggest reasons for caution . <p> First , despite their pro-Labor vote intention , the diaspora broadly supports Morrison , thinks he has performed well as prime minister , and believe he has handled relations with India ably . Indeed , a plurality of respondents would like to see Morrison return as prime minister . <p> Second , when it comes to representing the interests @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the diaspora rates Labor only marginally higher than the Coalition . Indeed , perhaps because the community 's rapid growth is such a recent phenomenon , no party is seen as closer to the community . Roughly equal numbers of respondents perceived that Labor ( 27 per cent ) and the Coalition ( 25 per cent ) are " closer " to the Indian community , while 35 per cent felt they are the same . <p> Loading <p> The net result of this new survey evidence is that while Labor holds a distinct advantage over the Coalition among Australians of Indian origin , it should not rest on its laurels . For this group of immigrants , it is advantage Labor -- for now . <p> Caroline Duckworth and Milan Vaishnav are junior fellow and director , respectively , in the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington , D.C. Devesh Kapur is the Starr Foundation Professor of South Asian Studies at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies . Their new study on Indo-Australians can be found here .

The opposition has accused the government of a substantial national security failure after Solomon Islands signed a new security deal with China . <p> Loading <p> The Coalition has made several commitments to boost defence including $8 billion to build new helicopters , $58 million to expand defence manufacturing in Queensland , and $24 million to upgrade the Navy 's Marine Precinct in Cairns . It has also promised more than $180 million to facilitate pathways into the defence industry . <p> Labor has promised @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ back cutting-edge projects and technologies . And it has committed $135 million to trial urgent care clinics to relieve pressure on hospital emergency departments . <p> The Coalition has pledged $827 million to establish a National Comprehensive Cancer Network with " world-leading " treatment centres in Brisbane , Perth and Adelaide , modelled on Melbourne 's Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre . It 's also committed an extra $273.1 million to provide free continuous glucose monitoring @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ says his government has achieved " record levels of Medicare bulk-billing " and points to the growing health budget , but the number of Australians accessing bulk-billed GP services is falling . <p> Advertisement <h> Federal integrity commission <p> Both parties have proposed different models for a federal integrity commission . <p> Loading <p> The Coalition 's commonwealth integrity commission proposal was released in 2021 and met with widespread criticism due to its inability to hold public hearings , launch investigations , act on anonymous tips , or issue public findings . <p> The draft legislation has not been brought to the parliament yet , but the prime minister has said he is not interested in amending the model . <p> Labor has proposed its own national anti-corruption commission " with teeth " by the end of 2022 , which it expects will examine alleged misconduct from as far back as 15 years . This model can hold public hearings and publicly issue findings . <p> The Coalition announced a $2.4 billion plan to overhaul the apprenticeship training scheme in the budget . It also increased the subsidy level for younger siblings when a family has two or more kids aged under five in care at once -- a move expected to benefit 250,000 families . <p> Labor 's proposal is to lift the subsidy level for everyone using care and increase the means test so more families are eligible . Labor will make a submission to the Fair Work Commission if it wins government , warning against real wages going backwards . <p> The Coalition has criticised Albanese 's stance and says low unemployment will lead to wage growth . The prime minister has committed to reviving its shelved industrial relations omnibus bill , which includes criminalising wage theft . <p> Labor supports this measure but opposes other proposed reforms it warns will erode pay and working conditions under the guise of flexibility . <p> Labor would also abolish two federal watchdogs , the Registered Organisations Commission and the Australian Building and Construction Commission , with the Coalition warning such a decision would lead to lawlessness and economic loss . <h> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ line between Sydney and the Hunter , committed $2.2 billion for a suburban rail loop in Victoria , and promised $125 million to manufacture electric buses in Western Australia . <p> In the March budget , the Coalition also made some public transport promises including a fast rail from Sydney to Newcastle , but most of its election pledges involve upgrades for roads and highways in places like Nowra , Old Gympie Road and Epping . <h> Aged care <p> Labor pledged an extra $2.5 billion over four years to improve regulation and mandate 24/7 registered nurses by July 2024 , a year earlier than recommended by the royal commission , dependent on staff availability . <p> The Coalition is committed to the first stage of the recommended minimum staffing levels -- mandating a nurse on-site for 16 hours a day and an average 200 minutes of direct care a day per resident , including 40 minutes with an RN -- from October 2023 . <p> Both parties will look to migration to fill shifts . <p> Both parties would fund higher wages , but only Labor has committed to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ before the Fair Work Commission . @@90921702 <p> Australia is expected to get its sixth prime minister in nine years , with polls pointing to a win for Anthony Albanese 's Labor team . When polls open on Saturday , ballots will be cast for 1203 candidates across the 151 seats in the House of Representatives . As well , 421 Senate candidates are vying for 40 seats across the states and territories . When 6pm rolls around , the ballots of more than 17 million voters will start to be counted , including those of more than five million people who voted early . Scott Morrison 's Liberal-National government heads into the election holding 75 seats , having lost the WA seat of Stirling in a redistribution . Labor starts with 68 seats , plus notionally the new Victorian seat of Hawke . The major parties will need 76 seats for a majority in the lower house . Opinion polls are averaging 53.5 per cent to Labor on a two-party preferred basis , according to The Poll Bludger website , which if reflected at the ballot box would result in 83 seats for the ALP . The latest Newspoll , published in the Australian on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That 's despite a two point drop in the party 's primary vote to 36 per cent . Mr Morrison , who campaigned in Perth on Friday , said the election would be close . " Australians weigh up their decision very , very carefully , " the Liberal leader said . " What Australians will be wanting to know is what certainty and security can they have going forward for them and their families ? " Mr Albanese - who campaigned in South Australia , Tasmania and Victoria on Friday - said many people who had voted Liberal all their lives were now walking away from the party . " There 's three more years of the same , or there 's myself , who wants to bring the country together , who wants to be inclusive , who wants to end the division , " Mr Albanese said . The campaign has focused on the issues of cost of living , economic management , national security , a federal integrity commission , climate and equality and safety for women . Mr Albanese stumbled on economic questions in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the coalition 's attack over his inexperience . Mr Morrison 's economic credentials took a hit with a rise in the cash rate and the latest wages figures coming in well below inflation , while he sought to remodel his personal " bulldozer " style of leadership . Closely watched will be the success of the so-called " teal " independents running a well-funded campaign on climate change , integrity and women 's safety across a number of Liberal-held seats . Defeat for Labor will be the fourth successive loss and mean the ALP has won majority government only once in the past 10 elections . If Mr Morrison wins , he will be the first incumbent prime minister to win two elections in a row since John Howard in 2004 . The Liberal campaign has targeted the seats of Hughes , Gilmore , Parramatta , Hunter ( NSW ) , Lyons ( Tasmania ) , Corangamite ( Victoria ) and Lingiari ( NT ) . @@90921945 <h> Pursuit home <h> Why are we so vulnerable to bad information ? <p> Identifying misinformation is difficult for all of us , but we can make it easier by being aware of our biases and wary of strong emotions <p> By Associate Professor Andrew Perfors , University of Melbourne <p> Share selection to : <p> There are two fundamental reasons why misinformation is a bigger problem than ever before . <p> The first is tied to rise of the internet and social media . Where once only the richest and most powerful could spread their ideas widely , now the vast majority of people can do so at the click of a button . <p> Socia media as made it easier to both discover truth and spread lies . Picture : Shutterstock <p> This empowerment of those who were once voiceless can be a very good thing . But now malign actors can also influence enormous numbers of people in almost all parts of the globe . <p> Anybody from a foreign power to a politician to a company can inject huge quantities of bad information into the system -- reaching millions of people in a fraction of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bad information is hard <p> This itself would n't be the problem it is if it were n't for the other factor -- which is that for a lot of reasons , people are n't great at figuring out what information to believe . <p> This is because the task of identifying bad information is enormously difficult and the proverbial dice are loaded heavily against us . <p> Lies are much easier to weed out if you can check them against your own direct evidence or experience . This is why nobody lies about commonly observable things like the colour of grass or the legal driving age . <p> Unfortunately , most things in the media ca n't be verified by us firsthand . Did Trump engineer a coup ? Are vaccines safe ? Is climate change real ? Even if we have access to real data at scale ( which hardly ever happens ) almost none of us have the expertise or time to evaluate it well . <p> Combine these tendencies with the fact that emotions short-circuit our reasoning , and it is easy to see that false @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ appeals to our social group , will spread much faster and much further than a boring truth . <p> This makes us see it more often , and this increased frequency makes us believe it even more . <p> Where is the role of rationality in all of this ? <p> We are certainly capable of evaluating the truth of a thing based on whether it makes sense . But without direct access to the truth , the best we can do is analyse and interpret information from people who claim to have that data ( who might be lying ) . <p> We do that by seeing if their information is consistent with our other beliefs , as our beliefs are n't isolated chunks of knowledge but comprise of a thick web of interconnected theories , ideas and premises . <p> When that web is broadly correct , then analysing new information by comparing it against what we already know is a very sensible thing to do . <p> False news that makes us angry or scared will spread much faster and much further than a boring truth . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ undone , however , when people are exposed to information that mixes lies with truths , or when the falsehoods support an emotional need to believe some things over others ( as we see with the persistent refusal by some to accept that climate change or COVID-19 exist ) . <p> In an effort to buttress those needs , it 's possible to get sucked so far into a web of misinformation that the entire belief set is incorrect . <h> Be aware of your own biases <p> When your premises are false , only further falsehood makes sense . The end result is that people start believing in conspiracy theories and seem to inhabit an entirely different reality . <p> Truly , this is a wicked problem and many of the solutions are systemic . Somehow , truthful and correct things need to get shared more widely and more quickly . <p> There are some things us as individuals can do -- the main one is to be aware of these biases in ourselves . When you find yourself feeling strong emotions , that is often a sign that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ yourself in the shoes of the person who wrote or shared the information ; ask yourself what their agenda is . <p> If something sounds unbelievable or oversimplified -- that is another cue to try to confirm it independently . <p> Recognise your own fallibility and be humble -- you will get things wrong , but if your worldview is n't entirely entrenched in falsehoods , you 'll be much more likely to get the important things right . <p> How do you reach someone who is fully absorbed by conspiratorial beliefs ? <p> Recognising your own biases and fallibilities can help us to sift the false from the true . Picture : Getty Images <p> You wo n't win somebody over with facts ; instead , try to understand what emotional purpose their beliefs serve and see if you can give them other ways of meeting those needs , like offering support and connection . <p> It 's hard , long , aggravating work and is much more effective to identify people before they are pulled in too far . <p> More broadly , be kind . <p> It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ particularly our negative ones like fear and anger , in times ( like now ) when there is so much uncertainty , pain , and difficulty . <p> The more we can build strong bonds and trust with each other , the more we can fight the pull of the falsehoods and exaggerations that try to tear us apart . <p> Discover more by subscribing to PsychTalks on apple , google , spotify or wherever you get your podcasts . <p> Hosted by award-winning journalist Lynne Malcolm , this exciting new podcast series unpacks today 's big issues from the perspective of psychology research . @@90945267 <h> The Liberals ' post-election endgame <p> The election result has thrown Robert Menzies ' Liberal Party into an existential crisis . <p> Just hours into vote-counting , it was clear that the Coalition had not just lost government , but the Liberal Party had been decimated in its own heartland . <p> Huge swings , ranging from 5 per cent to 13 per cent were recorded in the Liberal Party 's traditional crown jewel seats -- Kooyong , which was Menzies ' old electorate , plus Higgins , Goldstein , Wentworth , Mackellar , North Sydney and Curtin . <p> Nearly 80 years after Menzies formed the Liberal Party , which went on to hold power in the national parliament for 51 of the next 76 years , the Scott Morrison-led Liberal Party has been pole-axed by a tectonic shift in Australian politics . It is one where affluent , professional voters , particularly women , are placing issues such as climate change , integrity in government , and respect for women , above more bread and butter concerns such as the economy . <p> In an election that took on the appearance of 151 byelections , or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ states , there was a dramatic shift towards independents and Green candidates in more affluent seats in Sydney , Melbourne , Brisbane , Perth and Adelaide , while the Coalition parties performed better in outer suburbs , regional and rural areas . <p> As results came in , finance minister and SA Liberal senator Simon Birmingham commented on the ABC : " There is clearly a big message and winning government without those seats ( like Wentworth , Warringah , North Sydney , Higgins , Goldstein and Kooyong ) is a next-to-impossible task . <p> " There are issues that we will have to clearly address and we have to have candidates that clearly understand those issues . " <p> In an unmistakable reference to the last-minute selection of hard-line Liberal candidates in NSW , including Katherine Deves in Warringah , enforced by Prime Minister Scott Morrison , Senator Birmingham acknowledged there had been " process breakdowns right across the board , and clear mistakes were made . We have paid a price for that . " <p> He called for the Liberal Party to show " respect for inclusion @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ party 's loss of the seat of North Sydney , which is located next to Warringah , where Deves ran a campaign featuring criticism of transgender athletes engaging in female sporting events , Birmingham said figures such as defeated Liberal moderate Trent Zimmerman in North Sydney were " being punished by association " . <p> " Gender clearly is a factor in this . In every seat , the Liberal Party has lost to a female candidate . That is a very clear message . " <p> Amid the electoral cross-party carnage , a " a pox on both your houses " mood was also hurting Labor , albeit less severely . ALP shadow treasurer Jim Chalmers said that although " the big move has been the rejection of Scott Morrison , we 're not immune from this independents challenge " . <p> Katherine Deves ' controversial opinions on transgender women in sport made Warringah the focal point of a national transgender debate . Later , independent , and former world champion slalom ski champion , Zali Steggall won Warringah from former Liberal prime minister Tony Abbott in the May 18 , 2019 , election . <h> Losing the crown jewels <p> But on Saturday night , the Liberal Party lost its electoral crown jewels in Australia 's two most populous states , as it also lost office . <p> The background is decades of faction fighting in the NSW Liberal Party , which turned rancid in the past seven years with the destruction of Tony Abbott 's prime ministership by Turnbull , followed by Turnbull 's removal , and the emergence of independents in 2018-19 . <p> More recently , there was the intervention by the prime minister and former NSW Liberal Party director , Scott Morrison , in the pre-selection process . @@90945729 <h> The race you should be watching on Saturday night <h> Federal election 2022 <p> Election campaigns in Australia focus , almost exclusively , on the contest for seats in the House of Representatives . As psephologists , pollsters , political scientists and journalists , we are practised at tracking voting intention for the House and voters ' preferred prime minister , but we pay relatively little attention to the contest for the Senate . <p> There are a few reasons for this . The House is where governments are formed , party leaders and prime ministers are chosen , and representatives elected to give a voice to the people . <p> Little attention is given to the Senate because the House is where government is formed and the prime minister is chosen.Credit:Alex Ellinghausen <p> The Senate , originally conceived as the states ' house , has functioned in practice as a house of review . <p> The system of preferential voting used to elect members of the House produces a result that can be predicted ahead of time and can , more often than not , be declared on election night . <p> The proportional system used to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by citizens and can take days , sometimes weeks , to produce a clear result . <p> The relative inattention that the Senate receives during election campaigns sits uneasily with the role and influence of this chamber in Australian democracy . The extent of this influence depends directly on who is elected . <p> The proportional voting system used in the Senate means it can take weeks to get a result.Credit:Courtesy AEC <p> For much of its history , the Senate has not been controlled by governments . This is by design , rather than by chance . The Senate 's electoral system , proportional representation , enables the election of a more diverse range of parties and Independents than we typically see in the House . This is exploited by a sizeable proportion of Australian voters -- 30 per cent in 2019 according to Australian Election Study data -- who strategically vote for a different party in each house . <p> For all the talk of minority government and the teal independents holding the balance of power in the House , we are almost assured that any government -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crossbench Senators to pursue its legislative agenda . What this might look like after Saturday is particularly interesting . <p> Advertisement <p> Currently , the Coalition and Labor hold 61 Senate seats between them . The remaining 15 seats are shared between the Greens ( with nine seats ) , Pauline Hanson 's One Nation ( with two seats ) , the Jacqui Lambie Network , Centre Alliance , the Rex Patrick Team and the Liberal Democrats . Pauline Hanson is up for election , as are Rex Patrick and Stirling Griff ( both formerly of the Nick Xenophon Team ) and Green senators from Tasmania , Victoria and Western Australia . <p> The most interesting contests are occurring in Tasmania , the ACT , Queensland and South Australia . In Tasmania , the Jacqui Lambie Network is aiming for a second representative at the expense of Liberal Eric Abetz . In the ACT , Climate 200-backed independent David Pocock is a strong challenger to disrupt the longstanding pattern of Labor and Liberal holding one seat apiece . In Queensland , the Senate competition is fierce , with Pauline Hanson @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ premier Campbell Newman , who is running for the Liberal Democrats . In South Australia , while Nick Xenophon is returning to the ballot , the Greens and Labor are optimistic of their chances of picking up extra seats . <p> One Nation leader Pauline Hanson is in battle in Queensland against the Greens , Clive Palmer and Liberal Democrat candidate , the former state premier Campbell Newman.Credit:James Brickwood <p> In policy terms , two possible scenarios are likely to arise from Saturday 's election . The first is the potential shift to a more progressive Senate . This would be achieved if Labor 's increased popularity in the House also flows through to its Senate vote , which is possible in states such as South Australia , Victoria and Western Australia . If a consistent proportion of voters continue to vote for the Greens as their alternate party in the Senate , we might see that party pick hold their existing three seats and pick up another in South Australia . There is also a real chance that David Pocock is elected in the ACT . The alignment of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has the potential to create a unique window of opportunity to pursue more proactive legislation on transitioning to a greener economy . <p> The second scenario would see a more complex constellation of actors with the balance of power distributed between Hanson , Lambie , Xenophon and Palmer . While there is a temptation to categorise senators into progressive and conservative camps , in many ways the issues on which these senators campaign defy clear ideological alignments . <p> Loading <p> Jacqui Lambie , for instance , has publicly doubted the science behind climate change but also supported bolstering Tasmania 's renewable energy sector . The Palmer United Party is campaigning on a platform of increased funding for education and hospitals , while at the same time promising tax breaks . As fierce advocates for their states and a diverse range of causes , legislative negotiations with these senators become complex for a government of any type as their voting patterns and allegiance are less predictable . <p> The continued practice of split ticket voting among a sizeable proportion of Australians suggests that many do not share the sentiments of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unrepresentative swill " or John Howard 's assertion that it is a " house of obstruction " . The contest for the Senate brings to the fore debates between majority will and diversity , between legislative certainty and accountability . It is a battle that we need to pay more attention to . <p> Anika Gauja is professor in the School of Social and Political Sciences , Sydney University .

@@90964075 <h> Federal election 2022 <p> On the Monday evening before the election , Jason Falinski , the federal member for the Sydney seat of Mackellar , is standing in a darkening suburban car park handing out fliers to every last straggler turning up at the local pre-poll station before it closes at 8pm . <p> As he 'll later tell TheSydney Morning Herald and TheAge , there were 127 hours of pre-poll voting in his electorate -- and he was there for 124 ? of them , every bit of it " trench warfare " . <p> Falinski 's desperate hunt for votes that night turns out to have been a harbinger of the broader existential crisis that now threatens to engulf the Liberal Party . <p> Until Saturday 's shock election result , his seat , centred on Sydney 's mostly prosperous northern beaches , would have counted as Liberal heartland . The party had held it continuously for 73 years , and his margin of 13.3 per cent from the last election would normally have been judged unassailable . <p> But no one knows what the new Liberal normal looks like any more . Their teal branding derives from independent Zali Steggall 's successful raid on Tony Abbott 's former seat of Warringah in 2019 . <p> Besides Scamps , the victorious teal contingent appears to include Dr Monique Ryan in Kooyong in Victoria ( who seems set to take this former Liberal jewel from the man previously seen as party heir apparent , Josh Frydenberg ) ; former ABC foreign correspondent Zoe Daniel who has taken the Victorian seat of Goldstein from moderate Liberal MP Tim Wilson ; Allegra Spender , who 's won from Dave Sharma the ultra-well-heeled seat of Wentworth ( former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull 's onetime bastion ) ; Kylea Tink ( who boasts pink , not teal as her battle colours ) , who has unseated Trent Zimmerman ( again a moderate Liberal ) in the harbourside seat of North Sydney ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Fred Chaney , who is expected to snare another Liberal prize , the seat of Curtin in WA . <p> These are accomplished women , Malcolm Turnbull said , that " any political party would count as an enormous plus to have among their number . He says the scale of " this disaster for the Liberal Party " ca n't be overstated . <p> " These are the seats which had not only been ultra-safe but where the party raised most of its money , where it had the most members -- literally the Liberal Party bedrock , " he says . <p> " The message very clearly to the party now is , given these historically rolled-gold seats have moved to the crossbench , how does the Liberal Party ever get to form a majority in its own right ? " <p> Advertisement <p> The fracturing of the party 's vote in wealthier metropolitan electorates amounts to what La Trobe University political historian Professor Judith Brett calls a " significant class defection " from the party founded by Robert Menzies in the immediate aftermath of World War II . <p> The federal Liberal Party faces a fundamental identity crisis . What does it stand for ? Who is it appealing to ? Where does its future lie ? Does it ( as many moderates believe it should ) evolve towards becoming a more socially progressive party with strong and credible aspirations on climate and women , while returning to a more conventional small " L " liberal , free-market economic policy ? <p> Or does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ peri-urban electorates , wooing them with populist right-wing stances on economic and social policy ? <p> In the immediate aftermath on Sunday morning , shell-shocked Liberals were divided about whether the party should tack further to the right or move to the centre as the rebuilding process gets under way . @@90964117 <h> Editorial <h> Albanese wins a clear mandate for inclusive but cautious change <p> Political scientists say that many countries hold elections , but the true test of democracy is whether the elections change the government . <p> That is why all Australians should be proud that our democratic institutions have once again functioned so smoothly and allowed for a seamless and uncontested transfer of power . After the storming of the Capitol in the US in 2021 , it is an achievement worth celebrating . <p> Anthony Albanese , with his partner Jodie Haydon and son Nathan , claiming victory on Saturday night . " I will lead a government worthy of the people of Australia , " he said.Credit:Janie Barrett <p> In this case , the Herald also believes that the change of government is in the best interests of Australia . Labor leader Anthony Albanese is not just offering different policies but also an end to the toxic zero-sum politics of the past decade . He said in his acceptance speech he would promote " unity and optimism , not fear and division " . <p> Albanese has a clear mandate to end the fake culture @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fuelled by some sections of the media -- which have set city against country and progressives against conservatives . <p> A strong majority of Australians have clearly said they want stronger action on climate change . They want politicians to stop inflaming social tensions as Prime Minister Scott Morrison did with his focus on transgender sportspeople during the campaign . <p> Former finance minister Simon Birmingham on Sunday got it exactly right when he said that the Coalition 's failure to land a climate change policy and its opposition to same-sex marriage lost it this election . <p> Albanese should also end the stalemate that has too long delayed constitutional recognition of Indigenous people consistent with the Uluru Statement from the Heart and the creation of a powerful and independent national integrity commission . <p> He must deliver on his promise to give women real power in the cabinet , change the tone of public debate on women 's issues and break up the Canberra boys ' club . <p> While his mandate on these matters is clear , the limited nature of Albanese 's election victory counsels caution in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he must not let the crossbench dictate his policies . They have a role to play but they are not representative of the broader Australian public . <p> Advertisement <p> Even if he wins a majority , he should reflect on why only 32.8 per cent of voters listed the ALP as their first preference . <p> Loading <p> The figure is probably a slight underestimate because many Labor supporters in inner-city seats voted tactically for teals who they believed stood a better chance of beating Liberals . Still , it suggests not all voters are sold on Albanese 's program . <p> The main reason Albanese should be cautious , however , is because that is what he promised during the election . <p> He won back suburban seats in NSW , Victoria and WA precisely because he eschewed the " tax and spend " redistributive left-wing economic policies of his predecessor , Bill Shorten . <p> While he campaigned hard on aged care , free child care and Medicare , he also pledged to bring under control the trillion-dollar debt run up during the pandemic . <p> Unless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ during the election campaign -- he will have to limit his ambitions on welfare spending . It is a dilemma which could decide the success of his prime ministership . <p> While the ALP faces challenges , it is the Coalition which must do most soul-searching . The party has lost small " l " educated liberals and women in blue ribbon Sydney seats . It must decide whether it wants to regain them or move even further to the populist right . <p> Albanese , by contrast , has a great chance to restore the ALP to the position it held under Bob Hawke and Paul Keating as a centrist and progressive party of broad appeal . He has won a historic victory which gives him a mandate for cautious , inclusive change . <p> The Herald 's View -- Since the Herald was first published in 1831 , the editorial team has believed it important to express a considered view on the issues of the day for readers , always putting the public interest first .

@@90964367 <h> How a low-key campaign delivered a prime minister who can raise expectations <p> Anthony Albanese started to sound like a leader capable of showing that his party had a Labor soul . Picture : AAP . <p> Labor 's successful bid for government - only its fifth victory from opposition since the first world war - was based on an experiment that no one could have known would work . <p> It was a small-target strategy of a kind that has never seen Labor come from opposition to government at an election in the federal sphere . It offered a low-key campaign , led by a man with 25 years of parliamentary experience . Most of the media pack proclaimed this another of Albanese 's gaffes . <p> But many of this country 's journalists display little feel for public sentiment - as they showed when they famously misread the import of Julia Gillard 's misogyny speech - and on this occasion they failed to see that Albanese had for the first time established his campaign 's central thread . <p> It was a rather modest claim : that low-paid workers should not suffer a further decline in their living standards . But it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to welfare . <p> Alongside its support for targeted , means-tested support , Labor has long supported certain types of universal provision - going right back to its maternity allowance of 1912 . Medicare was another example . @@90964462 <p> " For a left-wing party in power , its most serious antagonist is always its own past propaganda , " wrote George Orwell on the last pages of his final notebook . It was true in 1950 and is true today . <p> Can a party that once treated climate change as the greatest moral challenge of our times satisfy supporters with a 43 per cent cut to greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 ? Can a party that promised higher wages satisfy workers by holding an employment summit ? Can a leader who vowed to create more manufacturing jobs actually do that ? <p> Advertisement <p> A close look at the Albanese agenda shows he has kept his promises in check even when his rhetoric has soared . <p> Albanese has bristled at the repeated claim that he was a small target in this campaign . It is true that his softly persuasive catchphrase of " safe change " was deliberately cautious but also true that calling the policies " small " was and is unfair . <p> On climate , for instance , the gulf between Labor and the Coalition was not measured merely by the gap @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Albanese took the risk of endorsing a mechanism with an implicit price on carbon by modifying the existing " safeguard mechanism " to put an obligation on big companies to cut their emissions . This is a serious difference to the Coalition approach of spending taxpayer money to subsidise those same companies . <p> On integrity , Labor advances a far more powerful commission to investigate corruption with a model that matches the calls from expert groups like the Centre for Public Integrity and Transparency International , as well as the open letter from 31 former judges last week . It is a significant commitment . <p> On gender equity , Albanese promises to act on all recommendations of the Respect@Work report and place a positive duty on employers to prevent discrimination . Whether this is a " small " undertaking or not might depend on whether someone has ever suffered discrimination . The key point is that Albanese goes where Morrison would not . <p> On the minimum wage , Labor pledges to ask the Fair Work Commission to increase the base pay for workers . Albanese says @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but made sure to add that this does not apply to millions of workers whose award rates are linked to the minimum wage . He has clearly raised expectations , however , and must find ways to increase real wages . <p> On childcare , the Labor policy is concrete and deliverable : a $5.1 billion outlay on greater subsidies to lower the cost for families . Expect it to be one of the first items on the agenda . <p> Expectations are low on other fronts . State premiers want at least $5 billion to shore up emergency departments in the recovery from the pandemic , but Albanese has merely promised to talk . <p> And economic reform ? Albanese set out an agenda in a speech to the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry in the fourth week of the election campaign . He did not mention tax reform and has buried the Labor tax agenda from the last election , but he emphasised measures like childcare to expand the workforce . <p> Loading <p> This looks far too modest for economic hard-heads who want the incoming prime @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , which he thinks should be able to lift wages and profits in tandem by boosting productivity . This is a key area where he has raised hopes while being vague about how he will deliver results . <p> Over and over , Albanese has said he wants to under-promise and over-deliver . He has been cautious with his commitments - too cautious , in fact , for many Labor supporters . Some have gone to the Greens for this very reason . <p> This might explain why Albanese has also talked about an agenda that could take two terms to put into effect , another way of urging people to be patient . If there is change under this government , it is likely to come slowly . <p> Orwell knew the danger for a progressive party leader in raising unrealistic expectations . Albanese seems to know it , too .

But with a variety of changes to address the errors of 2019 , polling continues . Newspapers such as ours do it , the political parties do it and rely on it in part to see how they are travelling , and independent pollsters are also in the field . <p> Seat by seat polling , which tries to work out how individual candidates are doing , should be treated with particular caution because of their small sample sizes . On the ABC 's Media Watch on Monday night polling analyst Kevin Bonham said such polling " should be treated with great caution " , and Australian National University politics senior lecturer Jill Sheppard , said it was " almost impossible " for pollsters to reliably identify and contact the population they wanted to survey . <p> A thumping victory for Daniel ? Credit:Darrian Traynor <p> Which brings us to a poll in Goldstein released this week by the Australia Institute . They are left-leaning but not being paid by either of the parties , and they have given us the full results of their poll , so we can see their working out , which is why we 're even having this conversation . <p> The poll shows such a thumping victory for Zoe Daniel on May 21 that both candidates are playing it down . It has a primary vote for Daniel of 35 per cent and incumbent Liberal Tim Wilson on 34 per cent , which would be a dramatic , almost unbelievable , 20 per cent collapse in Wilson 's primary vote from 2019 . <p> Once the pollsters , uComms distribute preferences , most of which will flow from Labor and the Greens to Daniel , it points to a two party preferred result of Daniel 62 per cent to Daniel and Wilson 38 per cent . ( Using a different method of distributing preferences the figure was 57 per cent to 43 per cent for Daniel ) . Even the Australia Institute 's director , Ben Oquist , said he suspected this result " may be slightly optimistic " for the independent . <p> The poll also found that voters were evenly divided over whether Daniel should support Labor or the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament . <p> On the ABC this morning Daniel agreed that anyone who watches politics and polling knows that it 's " very difficult to reliably poll individual seats " . Nonetheless , she said it was " encouraging " and showed many Goldstein voters " want to shake things up " . <p> Wilson said : " Just add it to the list of outsiders trying to change our community from GetUp 's stunts , Extinction Rebellions graffiti , Climate 200 's chequebook and now the Australia Institute 's polling from a union outfit just to get a so-called ' independent ' elected to sneak Labor into government " . <p> The uComms poll of 855 voters was conducted on Wednesday night last week . Among the remaining candidates - nine have nominated - the poll had the ALP 's Martyn Abbott on a 14 per cent primary vote and the Greens candidate Alana Galli-McRostie on 8 percent . There were 6.3 percent of voters undecided . <p> The Goldstein poll follows another uComms poll this month that found treasurer Josh Frydenberg faced losing his seat of Kooyong to independent , Monique Ryan . The process involves an official announcement of the final line up of candidates followed by a bingo-like draw to determine the order on the ballot . <p> The Goldstein ballot as drawn on Friday <p> Nine candidates have nominated , with previously undeclared hopefuls from the Liberal Democrats , Derryn Hinch 's Justice Party and the Sustainable Australia Party , making late entries into the race . <p> While the Greens are not running hard in Goldstein -- " teal " independent Zoe Daniel has stolen their thunder -- their candidate Alana Galli-McRostie was delighted to draw number one because that will give her the best spot to pick up donkey votes . " Every vote counts , " she says . <p> Independent psephologist Dr Kevin Bonham says the advantage of donkey votes -- where people number the ballot in consecutive order from top to bottom -- was less than 1 per cent in most seats . <p> Of the main candidates , Daniel did best . She was drawn at number 5 on the ballot ahead of main rival incumbent Tim Wilson who is down in 8th spot . Wilson says he is relaxed about his poor poll position . " Getting excited about ballot order is pseudo mysticism , " he says . But is it really time for Goldstein , named after Vida Goldstein , an early suffragist who unsuccessfully contested five elections as an independent early last century ? <p> It 's a big ask . <p> Goldstein -- formerly known as Balaclava -- is among the bluest of blue ribbon Liberal seats , held since federation 121 years ago by conservative MPs , all male . <p> In the 1940s , an independent , Arthur Coles , did hold Henty , which took in a small part of the seat , but since Coles the whole of Melbourne has had just one independent federal MP -- left-wing footy hero Phil Cleary in Wills in the 1990s . <p> Melbourne has had only one female independent federal MP , Doris Amelia Blackburn , who held the seat of Bourke from 1946 to 1949 . <h> The Golden Mile <p> The Royal Brighton yacht club is at the southern end of the Golden Mile , a strip of leafy streets and mansions with easy beach access , one of Melbourne 's wealthiest neighbourhoods . Goldstein is among the country 's wealthier electorates with a median weekly household income of $2018 according to the 2016 census , well above the Australian average of $1438 . <p> More than 43 per cent of Brighton residents have bachelor degrees or higher , twice the national average . There are more non-religious residents here than the Australian average , but 6.8 per cent describe their religion as Judaism , well above the national average of 0.4 per cent . <p> The Liberal vote is strongest in the well-to-do bayside neighbourhoods -- Brighton , Hampton , Sandringham , Black Rock and Beaumaris -- but softer in the more modest inland suburbs of Bentleigh , McKinnon and Highett . <p> Tim Wilson first won the seat in 2016 by a record margin and retained it in 2019 with 52 per cent of the primary vote despite a swing against him . <p> He cut his political teeth at Monash University 's student union and as a policy director with the free market think tank , the Institute of Public Affairs ( IPA ) , and is now often described as a " moderate " or " modern " Liberal , but says he prefers just " liberal " . <p> He was prominent on issues such as same-sex marriage and proposed to his partner , Ryan , on the floor of the House of Representatives . But his stance on issues such as softening section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act and for tinkering with superannuation , have led critics to query his moderate credentials . <p> Duelling campaign signs in Sandringham . Credit:Photo : Joe Armao <p> Daniel says the Goldstein " incumbent " is not a " moderate Liberal " . " He votes every time with Barnaby Joyce . This is not representing the people of Goldstein . " <p> If he is to prevail again Wilson needs to hold on to bayside Liberals , a group often characterised as well-educated , small-l Liberals interested in issues such as the environment and refugees in the tradition of the original Goldstein MP and Fraser-era frontbencher , Ian Macphee . <p> Daniel is banking on these same voters being sufficiently disillusioned by the long , rightward shift of the party nationally to back a respectable , centrist independent . @@90965153 <h> Woodside 's fossil fuel focus could push our climate over the edge <p> Climate polluter Woodside is building its business strategy around the absurd notion that the very thing driving the climate crisis should continue as part of the emergency response , writes David Ritter . <p> THIS WEEK a group of executives , politicians , lawyers and others met in Brisbane to discuss how to increase human suffering and accelerate the destruction of the natural world . <p> The event was the 59th annual conference and exhibition of the Australian Petroleum Production and Exploration Association ( APPEA ) , which is the peak national body for Australia 's upstream oil and gas exploration and production industry . <p> The world 's top experts have called time on the oil and gas industry because it is one of the main drivers of climate change . According to the IPCC , if we are to have any hope of achieving the internationally-agreed Paris climate goal to limit global heating to 1.5 ? C , existing fossil fuel infrastructure can not be fully utilised . <p> The International Energy Agency ( IEA ) has indicated that there should be no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ onwards ) . Scientists have warned that humanity faces ' untold suffering ' if we do not begin reducing greenhouse gas emissions at emergency speed and scale . <p> Accordingly , the objective of APPEA should now be the permanent winding up of these industries at rates compatible with the internationally-agreed Paris climate goals , whilst individual oil and gas corporations should now be engaged in rapid transition planning . <p> Heavy focus should be on developing business strategies to pivot to new products and revenue streams as quickly as possible -- most obviously in the renewable energy sector . <p> Instead , most of the participants at the APPEA conference ( many of whom presumably must have children who may one day ask what their parents did during the years of breaking climate emergency , the years that really mattered to humanity ) would appear to be intent on continuing to perpetrate the wrongdoing of oil and gas exploration and expansion . <p> In a recent speech , Australian author Tim Winton spoke evocatively of fossil fuel companies " trafficking in cognitive distortion " . This willful perpetuation of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , slogans , graphics , advertisements and smugly confident presentations . <p> And so it is that Meg O'Neill , chief executive officer of Woodside fronted the APPEA shindig this week and claimed that " the imperative to decarbonise is as strong as it 's ever been " . This is the same Woodside that was recently singled out by the world 's largest investor engagement initiative on climate change as among the worst performers in Australia and globally . <p> It is difficult to overstate the immorality of such schemes at this stage of the game . @@90981678 <h> Federal Election 2022 <p> The 2022 federal election result was a resounding victory for climate populism over policy . Of spin over substance , of dividing when we need to be uniting , of trivialising challenging global economic reform into a patina of catchphrases and big , empty targets . <p> Climate populism portrays climate change as a question of will , a moral challenge . It 's true that ambition is necessary , but it 's not sufficient . Talking big targets is easy . These include emissions trading , tariff reform and maybe capacity markets . These are n't popular , but they are effective -- and were completely invisible in the populist climate buzz of the election campaign . <p> Because it can be unpopular , climate and energy policy requires policy constancy for decades . Albo has compared himself to John Howard -- having taken the leadership in the wake of his party losing an unlosable election , only to come back three years later to win on a modest platform against an unpopular incumbent . <p> But Howard won big in 1996 with a 45-seat majority , while Albo will have half that at best . He does n't have the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The risk for Labor on taking government is never doing too little , but rather doing too much . <p> And the cautious and pragmatic leadership Albo showed both as leader of the house and as opposition leader may , in an unexpected way , be exactly the approach the country needs coming out of a once-in-a-century pandemic buffeted by global economic and geostrategic headwinds . A steady hand on the tiller . <p> Advertisement <p> With that in mind , the new government 's focus should first and foremost be on restoring good government -- to rebuild state capacity , to deliver on political integrity , to keep faith with the Australian people by delivering on the agenda it promised them . <p> That may be a challenge given the internal Labor tensions that were restrained these past three years , and what will surely be a cabinet champing at the bit after almost a decade in the wilderness . <h> Deficits ' as far as the eye can see ' <p> By far the two most critical figures will be new Treasurer Jim Chalmers and new Finance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ government without good budget process . And you ca n't have good budget process without at least one powerful figure to enforce discipline on their colleagues . <p> After 15 years of political dysfunction , the federal budget is a shambles . It 's not so much the hundreds of billions in debt racked up during the pandemic , but rather the structural deficits as far as the eye can see because a succession of governments of both stripes have promised a whole lot of new spending without the taxes necessary to pay for it . <p> The perverse thing in the short run is that Chalmers and Gallagher will likely be gifted a massive bounty of new revenue , albeit temporary , due to the impact of Russia 's invasion of Ukraine on commodity prices . Their first test when they deliver their budget update later this year is whether they have the fortitude to bank every last dollar of that tax windfall . <p> Advertisement <p> Looking beyond that , the budget 's current assumption for productivity growth of 1.5 per cent -- which includes both the 1990s @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ provides a false sense of security about the sustainability of the public finances . To do so , they need to impose a strong set of fiscal rules and run a disciplined Expenditure Review Committee process . That should mean fully offsetting all new spending with new revenue or spending cuts elsewhere , and a cap on real growth in spending of 2 per cent per year . Any temporary revenue windfalls or cyclical spending declines must be banked . <h> Climate wars are over <p> The other major area of focus should be climate policy . Labor must remember the more players that are carved out , the greater the burden on the others . <p> Advertisement <p> And Labor 's plan to " rewire the nation " leaves me scratching my head . @@90981681 <h> Federal Election 2022 <p> Saturday 's election obviously shifts the balance of power in the Liberal Party to the right . With moderates such as Josh Frydenberg , Dave Sharma , Trent Zimmerman and others gone , the Liberal Party will be dragged further to the right on issues including climate change , national security and LGBT rights . That 's just arithmetic . <p> But there 's a subtler shift in the wind . With fewer people in the Liberal Party to stand up for centrist economic liberalism , the party could simply vacate the field and become a populist conservative party devoid of sensible economic thinking , as the Republicans have done in the United States . <p> If so , there may be nobody to hold the Labor government to account on economic policy . And the big question is whether -- unconstrained by an opposition that believes in markets -- the ALP will pursue Hawke-Keating-style Third Way policies , or drift toward democratic socialism ? <p> Consider for a minute one of Labor 's core campaign pledges . " Making things in Australia " could mean strategic manufacturing in industries where supply chain disruption @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ problems . <p> This is the case for having readily scaled-up pharmaceutical manufacturing in Australia . We ca n't be at the whim of global politics or public health when it comes to insulin or penicillin supply . And it could mean investments in battery or other technology at which Australia plausibly has a genuine comparative advantage . Such an approach gets a tick from centrist economists . <p> Advertisement <p> But " making things in Australia " could mean a return to 1970s winner-picking industry policy -- an approach that failed the world over . A number of other Labor policies are similarly open to interpretation . <p> Improving sluggish wages growth could come from improving productivity improvements , or it could come from mandating higher wages for certain worker or sectors . <p> And tackling " insecure work " could mean providing basic benefits -- like two weeks of taxpayer funded sick leave to workers in the gig economy -- or it could mean an all-out attack on platform companies such as Uber . <p> In other words , Labor 's economic policy could be a reprise of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ updated version of the 1990s , or a return to the 1970s . I , for one , hope it will be the former . And there is good reason to believe that it will . <h> We 're all capitalists now <p> First , Labor 's greatest success in governing over the past three-quarters of a century occurred during the Hawke-Keating years . During this time , Labor not only enacted the reforms that set Australia up for three decades of uninterrupted economic expansion , it developed a reputation for responsible economic management that had been in serious doubt before that . <p> Advertisement <p> Second , one of Labor 's proudest achievements from this time was the establishment of compulsory superannuation . This turned the bulk of the Australian population into shareholders as well as workers . Most Australians now have a meaningful financial stake in the success of our biggest companies . Class warfare is a lot less attractive when it partly involves declaring war on oneself . In a very real sense , we 're all capitalists now . <p> With that comes new discipline on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the retirement savings of workers . Obviously , that does n't mean that workers do n't care about their own pay and conditions , but there are real constraints on us-versus-them divisions that did n't exist thirty years ago . <p> Third -- and this was one of the few arguments from Scott Morrison that resonated during the campaign -- it 's true that to have a strong social safety net we need a strong economy . Expenditure on the NDIS is forecast to grow from $30.8 billion this year to more than $70 billion a decade from now . Defence spending is growing rapidly . Aged care needs additional funding . The list goes on . Government debt is modest by international standards , but we need fiscal consolidation so we can spend aggressively in the next crisis . <h> Budget windfall <p> The Labor Party knows full well that to sustain this spending requires strong economic growth and low unemployment . Increasing income taxes , for instance , might seem tempting , but it would slow growth and increase unemployment . <p> It 's also worth remembering that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Jim Chalmers will inherit a massive windfall for his first budget later this year . With coal at over $US400 ( $565 ) a tonne and iron-ore above $US120 a tonne , Chalmers will find a kind of reverse black hole in the budget . That windfall will permit , at least in the short term , increased spending as well as improvements to the budget bottom line . <p> Advertisement <p> That said , there will be challenges . A number of the big reforms that happened in the Hawke-Keating era were about getting the government out of the way . Financial deregulation , floating the dollar , privatising state-owned enterprises all fall into this category . There is n't much low-hanging fruit like this lying around these days . <p> Of course , other lasting legacies from this period involved building big things . Medicare , the Accord , and outlawing workplace gender discrimination are notable examples . But these were big , hard things to do . They required exceptional leadership . <p> The Australian economy is changing in the biggest way since 1980s globalisation . One @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ secular decline . Two others -- iron ore and tertiary education -- are under significant pressure . <p> Managing this transition involves enabling the private sector to adapt to changing circumstances . It also involves government helping to co-ordinate activities -- such as targeted strategic manufacturing -- that wo n't happen by themselves . It 's a task for economic liberalism , even if the Liberal Party is no longer in that game . <p> Richard Holden is professor of economics at UNSW Business School and President of the Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia . ' <p> Michael Gable , managing director of Fairmont Equities <p> Listed companies in the childcare sector , including the largest player G8 Education , and others such as Mayfield Childcare and Evolve Education , could benefit from the extra spending , which could see their shares climb . <p> " The childcare sector is the one that seems to have the most upside , " Gable says . <p> The effects of the new government 's emphasis on mitigating climate change , and supporting renewable energy and electric vehicles , could also have longer-term benefits for more patient investors . <p> Under the Powering Australia policy , Labor plans to reduce carbon emissions by 43 per cent by 2030 , and aim for net-zero by 2050 . its more usual 0.25 percentage point increase , in an effort to head-off inflation expectations . <p> The increase would almost certainly flow through to mortgage holders in the form of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Under my government , Australia will set a new target to reduce emissions by 43 per cent by 2030 , putting us on track for net zero by 2050 . " <p> It represents the first time since the Abbott government in 2015 that Australia has committed to increasing its 2030 emissions reduction target . the international stage . <p> The Australian Greens will send its largest ever parliamentary delegation to Canberra after backing a 75 per cent emissions reduction target for 2030 , while ' teal ' would have allowed Australia to short-cut its way to targets . <p> The Quad meeting is being hosted by Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida and is expected to see the four countries progress
